props.name: disabled
props.description: Announces the field as disabled. Does not disable the control itself.

props.name: error
props.description: The validation message. Its presence drives `aria-invalid`.

props.name: invalid
props.description: Marks the field invalid independently of whether `error` is set.

props.name: label
props.description: Label text. Becomes the accessible name of the control inside.

props.name: required
props.description: Marks the field required. Announced through `aria-required` on the control.

ai.summary: Labels, describes, and marks a form control the consumer already owns.
whenToUse: The control is a plain `<input>`, a third-party widget, or not one of ours
Several controls share one label and one error
You need label, description, and error wiring without a form-associated wrapper
whenNotToUse: The control is `sk-input`, `sk-textarea`, or `sk-select` — those render their own label, description, and error
You want a form-associated control — use Input; a Field is not form-associated and never submits
You need a layout wrapper with no labelling — use a plain container
ai.accessibility: Puts `aria-labelledby`, `aria-describedby`, `aria-invalid`, and `aria-required` on the **control**, because that is the element a screen reader is on when it announces them, and sets nothing else — `value`, `name`, `disabled`, and validity stay the control's own. The description and error ids are appended together, not one replacing the other: an error that silences the hint removes the format instruction exactly when the user needs it. `invalid` and `error` are separate, so a field can be invalid before the consumer knows why. `required` renders an asterisk that is `aria-hidden` and a visually hidden word, so a reader hears 'required' rather than a symbol. The error carries a glyph as well as colour (WCAG 1.4.1).
ai.example: <sk-field label="Workspace name" description="Lowercase letters and dashes."><input type="text" /></sk-field>
knownLimitations: The field is not form-associated: it never sets `name`, never calls `setFormValue`, and does not participate in submission
It adopts the first form control in its slot; a field wrapping several controls labels only the first
It draws no chrome of its own — a box around a control that already has one reads as two nested inputs
